title: Oklahoma judge admitted to citing fake ChatGPT cases in court order, investigators say

reading.body:
This is a fabrication failure at the point of drafting, where a generative model produced case citations that do not exist and those citations were carried into a signed court order. The judge used ChatGPT to help prepare the order, and the false citations survived into the document that reprimanded an attorney. The failure is not that the tool was used, but that its output was treated as verified authority inside a formal legal instrument.

The check that would have caught it is the ordinary one for legal writing: pulling each cited case and confirming it exists and says what it is claimed to say. That step sits with the person signing the order, and it did not happen before the order issued. The error surfaced only when the reprimanded attorney challenged the order at the Oklahoma Supreme Court.

What is established is that the judge admitted the use and the nonexistence of two citations, and that he later vacated the order. What is not established is any criminal liability: the attorney general's office reviewed the investigation and found the evidence does not support prosecution, and any disciplinary outcome before the bodies that handle judicial misconduct remains open.

reports.title: Oklahoma judge used AI in ruling that contained false citations, prosecutor says
Oklahoma judge used AI on order that cited cases that don’t exist
Oklahoma judge admitted to citing fake ChatGPT cases in court order, investigators say

summary:
An Oklahoma judge, Lawrence Wheeler, admitted to the Oklahoma State Bureau of Investigation that he used ChatGPT to help prepare a 2025 order in a child paternity case, and that two case citations in it do not exist. The order reprimanded attorney Michael Beason, who challenged it at the Oklahoma Supreme Court, saying it relied on two nonexistent cases. Wheeler later vacated the order and is no longer on the case.

The state attorney general's office reviewed the investigation and decided the evidence does not support criminal prosecution. The matter could still go to the Oklahoma Court on the Judiciary or the Oklahoma Supreme Court, which handle judicial misconduct and can remove or discipline judges. Wheeler, 41, was elected in 2022 and was unopposed this year.
